strengths: Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over prior work (85.1 vs 76.1 on Town05 Long, 89.7 vs 64.3 on Town05 Short)
Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates why uncertainty matters in driving and demonstrates limitations of deterministic planning (Figure 1 is compelling)
Comprehensive technical approach integrating perception (map/agent/traffic tokens), prediction, and planning with multiple well-designed supervision signals
Solid experimental methodology with appropriate benchmarks, ablation studies isolating component contributions, and open-loop evaluation
Uses only camera input while achieving state-of-the-art, demonstrating advantage over LiDAR-dependent methods
Clear and well-organized presentation with effective motivating figures and logical method description
Achieves stable closed-loop operation without rule-based wrapper, supporting end-to-end driving claims
weaknesses: Limited novelty with mostly incremental improvements over VAD: scene encoding, token-based perception, and trajectory sampling are from prior work
Evaluation limited to CARLA simulation only with no real-world validation, severely limiting practical impact for safety-critical autonomous driving domain
Probabilistic planning contribution not sufficiently isolated: ablations show distribution loss matters but don't prove probabilistic paradigm drives improvements versus architectural changes
No comparison with deterministic baseline of identical architecture to quantify value of probabilistic vs. deterministic formulation
Action discretization lacks analysis: vocabulary size (4096) appears arbitrary with no sensitivity study; assumption that probability is continuous for discrete samples is stated but never validated
Reproducibility concerns: training hyperparameters missing (learning rate, optimizer, epochs, loss weights), no code release, censored demo URL
Conflict loss supervision assumes accurate agent motion predictions, but errors would provide misleading training signal; impact not analyzed
Methodological gaps: KL divergence choice not justified relative to alternatives; loss function weighting scheme not specified; no analysis of discretization approximation error
Inference strategy ambiguity: claims 'fully end-to-end' but discusses rule-based wrapper; unclear if main results use wrapper
Limited scope: trained on Towns 03,04,06,07,10 and tested on Town05; no cross-dataset evaluation or generalization analysis

strengths: Strong empirical results on CARLA Town05 benchmarks (85.1 driving score, 98.4% route completion), showing substantial improvements over prior work
Clear and well-motivated problem formulation with effective illustrations of why deterministic planning fails in multi-modal scenarios
Comprehensive system design integrating perception, prediction, and planning with appropriate supervision signals for each component
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (Table 3) demonstrating contribution of key components
Generally clear presentation with good visual explanations (Figures 1-2)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: probabilistic modeling for autonomous systems is not new; prior motion prediction methods model continuous distributions probabilistically. The claim of being 'first' for continuous planning is overstated
Core technical contribution is straightforward—discretizing action space and applying MLP with positional encoding—lacks methodological innovation
Action space discretization to 4096 trajectories is insufficiently analyzed: no ablation on vocabulary size, no comparison of discretization methods, quantization errors not discussed
Evaluation limited to CARLA simulation only; unclear if strong simulation performance translates to real-world driving given perfect sensing and controlled scenarios

Critical gap in experimental analysis: no ablation on inference strategies (greedy vs. sampling), no analysis of when/why multi-modality helps, no failure case analysis, no comparison with probabilistic baselines

Technical details missing or unclear: probability normalization method not specified, KL divergence computation undefined, conflict loss not formally defined, loss weighting scheme vague, training hyperparameters absent
Fairness concerns in comparisons: some baselines use camera+LiDAR while VADv2 uses cameras only; paper claims 'fully end-to-end' but uses rule-based wrapper in practice

Insufficient analysis of attribution: performance gains could stem from richer supervision (conflict loss) rather than probabilistic modeling itself; no comparison of deterministic vs. probabilistic supervision with same architecture
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; no cross-dataset generalization evaluation; no real-world applicability discussion
Reproducibility issues: no code availability, missing training details (learning rate, batch size, optimizer, model architecture specifics), insufficient technical specification for reproduction

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation addressing inherent uncertainty in driving through intuitive examples and principled probabilistic approach
Strong experimental results achieving SOTA on CARLA Town05 benchmarks: Driving Score 85.1 vs 76.1 (DriveMLM) with camera-only input, outperforming multi-modal methods
Comprehensive experimental validation including 10+ baseline comparisons, thorough ablation studies, both closed-loop and open-loop metrics, and qualitative visualizations
Thoughtful system design with multiple supervision signals (distribution, conflict, and scene token losses) that effectively integrate safety constraints
Practical advantages of probabilistic formulation: richer supervision for all actions, multi-modal predictions, and flexible integration with rule-based/optimization methods
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and logical flow
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: scene encoding borrows from VAD, probabilistic field function from NeRF, and distribution learning is standard; core contribution is incremental combination of existing techniques
Insufficient analysis of discretization strategy: no justification for vocabulary size (4096), ablation on N, or analysis of action coverage; 'furthest trajectory sampling' lacks formal motivation
Evaluation exclusively on CARLA simulator with no real-world validation; paper acknowledges unknown effectiveness in real-world scenarios, creating significant generalization concerns
Overclaimed end-to-end autonomy: benchmark results use rule-based wrapper for comparisons; fully end-to-end results without wrapper not prominently reported
Critical uncertainty analysis missing: no calibration evaluation, no comparison of predicted vs. true action multimodality, unclear whether distributions capture meaningful uncertainty

Scene constraint mechanism insufficiently detailed: conflict detection procedure, loss weight assignment, and future trajectory generation for other agents not clearly explained, critical for safety claims
Reproducibility limited: loss function weights unspecified, computational requirements not discussed, hyperparameter sensitivity not analyzed, code/data availability not mentioned
No failure case analysis: ~1.6% incomplete routes unexplained, safety-critical failure modes not discussed, infraction types not analyzed
Unfair baseline comparison: DriveMLM uses cameras + LiDAR while VADv2 uses cameras only; training data and setup details may differ from baselines

strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks with significant improvements on safety-critical metrics (15.6% collision reduction on 3DGS benchmark, 85.1 DS on CARLA vs 76.1 DriveMLM)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4+ major benchmarks (CARLA, Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, NAVSIMv2, 3DGS-based) with both closed-loop and open-loop evaluation
Substantial real-world evaluation through 3DGS-based benchmark using 2000 hours of real driving data and 337 reconstructed environments, providing safety metrics grounded in realistic scenarios
Extensive and well-designed ablation studies (Tables 6-8, 10-13) clearly demonstrating the importance of each component, including probabilistic vs deterministic comparison
Clear motivation and well-articulated problem formulation with good intuition for when probabilistic planning outperforms deterministic approaches (Figure 1)
Technically sound methodology with well-justified design choices: sensible vocabulary sampling (Algorithm 1), reasonable positional encoding, multi-stage training losses
Well-structured presentation with clear methodology, good figures, and comprehensive results tables making the paper accessible and reproducible
Practical robustness with the model running stably in fully end-to-end manner without rule-based wrappers, and flexible inference enabling integration with optimization methods
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: scene encoder heavily reuses existing components (BEVFormer, MapTR, VAD), positional encoding directly borrowed from NeRF, and probabilistic modeling itself is not novel—contribution is primarily application rather than methodological innovation

Core claims about probabilistic planning benefits lack rigorous theoretical justification: open-loop improvements are modest (Table 8), deterministic baseline is simple MLP without stronger uncertainty baselines, and no clear isolation of whether improvements come from probabilistic modeling vs discretization

Insufficient analysis of learned uncertainty: limited visualization of predicted distributions, Table 6 shows Top-1 to Top-5 perform similarly suggesting weak multi-modality learning, missing analysis of confidence calibration and whether learned modes correspond to meaningful behaviors

Discretization and vocabulary mapping issues: continuous-to-discrete mapping via L2 distance is coarse, limited analysis of discretization error consequences, Table 10 suggests 4096 vocabulary is suboptimal but computational costs not discussed, no analysis of performance when ground truth is far from vocabulary elements

Modest improvements on multiple benchmarks: NAVSIM shows only 0.7 point improvement over Hydra-NeXt (89.3 vs 88.6), Bench2Drive only 1.8 points over ETA, and multiple recent methods (Hydra-NeXt, DiffusionDrive, WoTE) achieve comparable performance

Comparison and ablation gaps: deterministic baseline could be stronger, missing comparisons with uncertainty-aware and ensemble methods, no isolated ablation on conflict loss (Eq. 6 is quite simple), limited exploration of alternative vocabulary sampling strategies (Table 13 shows minor differences)

Missing analysis and details: computational breakdown not provided despite claims of comparable latency, real-world deployment mentioned but not detailed, code link missing, theoretical justification for why p(a|o) modeling is fundamentally better than E[a|o]+uncertainty approaches

Reproducibility concerns: missing code link, some architectural details vague (Transformer decoder φ design), 3DGS benchmark proprietary, real-world results in supplementary material only, evaluation mostly limited to similar urban scenarios

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (CARLA, NAVSIM, NAVSIMv2, 3DGS-based) with strong closed-loop results (DS: 85.1 on Town05)
Well-motivated problem formulation: clearly articulates advantages of probabilistic over deterministic planning for non-convex solution spaces
Extensive ablation studies examining vocabulary size, training data amount, component contributions, and robustness to traffic density
Clear system architecture with well-designed scene encoder combining BEV, map tokens, agent tokens, and traffic element tokens
Ability to generate multiple reasonable trajectory modes, more aligned with human driving behavior
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: scene encoder heavily borrows from existing work (BEVFormer, MapTR, VAD); probabilistic planning is standard behavior cloning applied to discrete actions; positional encoding technique from NeRF is minor technical detail

Weak deterministic vs. probabilistic comparison: open-loop results show nearly identical performance (L2: 0.223 vs 0.225), contradicting main claim; closed-loop improvements likely from architecture rather than probabilistic formulation; deterministic baseline appears suboptimal

Planning vocabulary design poorly justified: Algorithm 1 (furthest trajectory sampling) lacks principled justification; Table 13 shows competing strategies (k-means, K-disks) achieve comparable results; fixed vocabulary limits action space generalization

Conflict loss inadequately explained: definition of 'conflict' is vague; potential circular supervision (agent token predictions supervise conflict loss); critical importance shown in ablations (Table 7) but insufficient detail provided

Ground-truth distribution artificially binarized: for each frame, single best-matching action labeled 1, others 0; this is binary classification, not true distribution learning; discretization error not analyzed

Rule-based wrapper undermines end-to-end claim: Section 4.2 acknowledges using rule-based filtering and optimization-based post-processing; contradicts 'end-to-end' messaging; suggests learned policy alone insufficient

Unfair comparisons: DriveMLM comparison uses different modalities (cameras+LiDAR vs cameras only); real-world results relegated to supplementary material; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Limited analysis of learned distributions: no visualization or comparison of predicted vs ground-truth distributions; multimodality not rigorously validated; Figure 4 shows cherry-picked examples; unclear whether top-K outputs represent genuinely different modes

Reproducibility issues: code URL incomplete ('available at .'); loss weights in Eq. 7 not specified; Transformer decoder architecture not described; transformer layer count and other hyperparameters missing

Modest improvements in some settings: open-loop deterministic vs probabilistic nearly identical (Table 12); Table 8 shows density robustness with modest margins (e.g., high density PDMS: 1.9% difference); on NAVSIM vs other methods, improvements often <1 point

strengths: Strong empirical results with SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks (CARLA, NAVSIM, Bench2Drive) showing clear advantages of probabilistic over deterministic planning in closed-loop evaluation
Well-motivated approach addressing a real limitation of deterministic planning—handling uncertainty and non-convex feasible solution spaces in autonomous driving
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with thorough ablations (Tables 7-8, 10-13) demonstrating the importance of each component and robustness across traffic densities
Clean and practical system design combining multiple perception modules (BEV, map tokens, agent tokens) with a principled probabilistic planning head
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured paper that makes the contributions easy to understand
Good practical considerations: camera-only input, no HD map requirement at test time, streaming inference, and naturally multi-modal outputs
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (BEV encoder, map/agent tokens, positional encoding) are largely borrowed from prior work; planning formulation reduces to standard softmax classification, not a fundamentally new technique
Lacks experimental comparison with other probabilistic planning methods (Diffusion Planner, GoalFlow, DiffusionDrive) despite claiming advantages of probabilistic planning—this is a significant gap

Distribution learning via 'best match' action assignment is oversimplified: treating all non-matched actions as zero probability differs substantially from LLM token prediction and deserves more principled treatment

Real-world validation is limited—real deployment results relegated to supplementary material, main evaluation is simulation-based; acknowledged limitations (naive agent behaviors, insufficient realism) may not fully transfer to real world

Action discretization design choices lack thorough justification: why is 4096 the right size, and is furthest trajectory sampling optimal? Table 10 ablates size but doesn't provide principled design analysis
Conflict loss is ad-hoc (simple indicator + log loss without sophisticated reasoning); questionable whether hard binary collision detection during training accurately reflects planning constraints
Gap between stated approach (sample max probability action) and suggested real-world practice (top-K + rule-based filtering), undermining the 'end-to-end' claim
Missing analysis of failure modes, difficult scenarios, and when probabilistic planning provides largest benefits; no investigation of vocabulary coverage or discretization error implications
